items.title: UK GDPR, Article 6: Lawfulness of processing
items.locator: Art. 6(1)(a) to (f), 6(5) and 6(11); notes F3 and F14
items.quote: processing is necessary for the purposes of a recognised legitimate interest
items.why: The binding rule: processing is lawful only if at least one listed basis applies. Point (ea) was inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.70(2)(b), in force 19 June 2025 for specified purposes and 5 February 2026 otherwise (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(c)). Points (ea) and (f) are not open to public authorities performing their tasks. Banner on the date checked: no known outstanding effects.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22B: Restrictions on automated decision-making
items.quote: is carried out entirely or partly in reliance on Article 6(1)(ea)
items.why: The exclusion: a significant decision may not be taken solely by automated processing where the processing for it relies, wholly or partly, on recognised legitimate interests. It is limited to solely automated decisions. Inserted by the 2025 Act, s.80(1); in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(j)).

items.title: UK GDPR, Annex 1: Lawfulness of processing: recognised legitimate interests
items.quote: This condition is met where the processing is necessary for the purposes of responding to an emergency.
items.why: The closed list behind the new basis: disclosure to a body with a public task; national security, public security and defence; emergencies; crime; safeguarding vulnerable individuals. Nothing in it covers model training or commercial AI use. Inserted 5 February 2026 by the 2025 Act, Sch. 4 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(z6)).

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 8A: Purpose limitation: further processing
items.locator: Art. 8A(2) and (3); note F1. Read with Art. 5(1)(b) and 5(3)
items.quote: any link between the original purpose and the new purpose
items.why: The test when data collected for one purpose is reused for another, such as training a model on customer records. Lists the factors to weigh and the cases treated as compatible (including Annex 2). Article 5(3) adds that compatible processing is not lawful for that reason alone, so a basis is still needed. Inserted by the 2025 Act, s.71(5); in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(d)).

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure lawfulness in AI?
items.locator: Section 'What should we consider when deciding lawful bases?'; also 'How should we distinguish purposes between AI development and deployment?' and 'Can we rely on legitimate interests?'
items.quote: You must break down and separate each distinct processing operation, and identify the purpose and an appropriate lawful basis for each one
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. Says the basis should be decided before processing starts, documented, and not swapped later without good reason; treats development and deployment as separate purposes; goes through each basis for AI. The page carries a banner that it is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act and may change; latest update shown is 28 October 2024, so it does not mention recognised legitimate interests.

items.title: Information Commissioner's Office response to the consultation series on generative AI: The lawful basis for web scraping to train generative AI models
items.quote: Legitimate interests remains the sole available lawful basis for training generative AI models using web-scraped personal data based on current practices.
items.why: The regulator's settled position after consultation: only legitimate interests is realistically available for web-scraped training data, developers must show why other ways of collecting data will not do, and poor transparency makes the balancing test hard to pass. The page shows no date; an ICO blog of 12 December 2024 announces the report. Written before the 2025 Act; the ICO says its guidance will be updated to reflect it.

items.title: Legitimate interests: What is the 'legitimate interests' basis?
items.quote: It’s not enough for you to simply say that using personal information is in your legitimate interests.
items.why: The three-part test (purpose, necessity, balancing), which must be satisfied before the information is used. Updated 23 March 2026 for the 2025 Act. The companion chapter 'When can we rely on legitimate interests?' says the basis cannot be the default for everything; 'What else do we need to consider?' says a changed purpose calls for a compatibility check and a fresh assessment.

items.title: A guide to lawful basis: Recognised legitimate interest
items.locator: 'At a glance' and section 'When can we use recognised legitimate interest?'
items.quote: You can’t use recognised legitimate interest as your lawful basis if you want to make significant decisions about someone based solely on automated processing.
items.why: The regulator's plain-language account of the new basis: five conditions with pre-approved public-interest purposes, no balancing test but necessity still required, not available to public authorities performing their tasks, and not usable for solely automated significant decisions. Published 23 March 2026.

items.title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
items.locator: Paras 60 and 66; executive summary pp. 2 to 3 (three-step test; scenarios on unlawfully trained models)
items.quote: the GDPR does not establish any hierarchy between the different legal bases laid down in Article 6(1) GDPR
items.why: EU comparator, not binding in the UK. Applies the same three-step legitimate interest test to developing and deploying AI models, and says a deployer should check that a model it uses was not built by unlawfully processing personal data. Useful for groups operating in both jurisdictions.

items.title: Monetary Penalty Notice: Clearview AI Inc
items.locator: Para 3 (amount), para 4(ii) and para 68 (p. 29) on lawful basis
items.quote: The amount of the penalty is £7,552,800
items.why: Source of the figure. Enforcement on scraped images used for a facial recognition service; one of the listed infringements is the absence of any Article 6 basis. Not a generative AI training case. Status: the First-tier Tribunal set the notice aside on jurisdiction; the Upper Tribunal reversed that on 6 October 2025 ([2025] UKUT 319 (AAC)) and sent the case back; the ICO's news page records permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on 19 December 2025. The penalty is therefore not final.

items.title: Enforcement Notice: Serco Leisure Operating Limited
items.locator: Paras 29 to 33 and 39 (lawful basis); background sub-paragraph (e) on the timing of the legitimate interests assessment
items.quote: Serco cannot rely on Article 6(1)(f) as it has failed to demonstrate the necessity of the processing
items.why: A UK enforcement decision that tests a claimed lawful basis and rejects it. The employer relied on contract and legitimate interests for facial recognition and fingerprint attendance checks; the regulator found neither applied because less intrusive means existed and the balancing test gave too little weight to staff. The legitimate interests assessment was done after roll-out and after the regulator made contact. Limits: an enforcement notice, filed under 'regulator guidance' because the type list has no value for one; about biometric recognition of employees, not model training; the notice orders the processing to stop and is not a fine.

items.title: The Information Commissioner v Clearview AI Incorporated [2025] UKUT 319 (AAC)
items.locator: Summary of decision; Decision; the description of the system ending at para 43
items.quote: utilises 'crawlers' to 'scrape' the public-facing internet for images of human faces
items.why: The tribunal ruling behind the brief's figure. It holds that the UK regulator had jurisdiction over a United States company that scraped faces from the internet to build a machine-learning recognition service, and sends the substantive appeal back to be heard. So the question of whether there was any lawful basis can now be decided. Limits: decides jurisdiction only, not lawful basis; the quoted words are from the summary, which is not part of the decision; a further appeal was reported in December 2025 and its outcome was not checked in this pass. Used by another brief for a different passage.

items.title: Guidelines 1/2024 on processing of personal data based on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR (version 1.0, for public consultation)
items.locator: Para 9; executive summary, p. 2 (three cumulative conditions)
items.quote: Article 6(1)(f) GDPR cannot be considered as a legal basis "by default".
items.why: The European regulators' method for the legitimate interests test, in terms that match the criterion's second level: the basis may not be chosen automatically or stretched because it looks less demanding, and the assessment comes before the processing. Limits: the version adopted for public consultation; whether a final version has replaced it was not confirmed. EU guidance, not binding in the UK, and it does not cover the UK's recognised legitimate interests basis.

items.title: Relying on the legal basis of legitimate interests to develop an AI system
items.publisher: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL)
items.locator: Opening summary; section on the three conditions (legitimate interest, necessity, balance)
items.quote: Controllers will most commonly rely on their legitimate interests for the development of AI systems.
items.why: The most developed regulator guidance found on lawful basis for building AI. The French regulator accepts legitimate interests as the usual basis for development, subject to three conditions and safeguards, and recommends documenting the analysis; it lists interests that will not qualify. A more permissive tone than the UK regulator's 2024 position on web scraping. Limits: French regulator, EU GDPR; the page is a courtesy translation and says the French text prevails. Not binding in the UK.

items.title: Guidance on privacy and developing and training generative AI models
items.publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
items.locator: 'Top five takeaways', second and third points
items.quote: Just because data is publicly available or otherwise accessible does not mean it can legally be used to train or fine-tune generative AI models
items.why: International comparator. Australian law has no list of lawful bases, yet the regulator reaches the same practical point: public availability is not permission, sensitive information generally needs consent, and reuse of data already held for training must be within what people would reasonably expect. Limits: Australian Privacy Act, not UK law; regulator guidance, not a decision.

items.title: Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems
items.locator: Part I, executive summary (p. 3); Part III, sections 4 to 6 (pp. 5-9)
items.quote: organisations can rely on exceptions to consent under the PDPA, e.g., for business improvement or research purposes
items.why: Second comparator, chosen because it takes a different legal route to the same question. Singapore starts from consent and then allows named exceptions for developing and testing AI, with criteria for each. Useful contrast with the UK approach of choosing among bases. Limits: advisory, expressly not legally binding; Singapore law; covers recommendation and decision systems, not generative models.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 13: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
items.quote: the purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing
items.why: The binding rule that makes lawful basis a matter of record, not afterthought: at the point of collection the controller must tell the person the legal basis and, where it is legitimate interests, what those interests are. A basis chosen after launch cannot have been disclosed on time. Limits: applies to data collected from the person; data obtained elsewhere, such as scraped data, falls under Article 14, which was not read in this pass.

items.title: A Common Pool of Privacy Problems: Legal and Technical Lessons from a Large-Scale Web-Scraped Machine Learning Dataset
items.publisher: Rachel Hong and five co-authors (University of Washington and others), arXiv
items.locator: Section 7.3.1 'Lawful basis / consent'; contributions list in section 1
items.quote: this basis requires a balancing test weighing the impact on individuals' rights
items.why: Empirical audit of a 12.8 billion sample web-scraped training set, followed by legal analysis. The authors found personal information that filtering had not removed, including an estimated 136,000 or more images of CVs, and conclude that under the GDPR only legitimate interests or consent could support such a dataset, with the balance likely to go against the developer. Evidence for the 'training' limb of the criterion. Limits: read as an arXiv preprint (the page links a later conference version, not read); authors are US-based and the GDPR analysis is brief.

items.title: Generative AI in EU Law: Liability, Privacy, Intellectual Property, and Cybersecurity
items.publisher: Claudio Novelli, Federico Casolari, Philipp Hacker, Giorgio Spedicato and Luciano Floridi, arXiv
items.locator: Privacy and data protection section, list of seven problems and sub-section 1 'Legal basis for AI training on personal data'
items.quote: the appropriate legal basis for AI training; the appropriate legal basis for processing prompts
items.why: Working paper that treats the legal basis for training and the legal basis for the data people type in as two separate questions, which is the structure the criterion uses. Also notes that the transparency duty requires the basis to be stated. Limits: preprint (version 4, March 2024); journal publication not confirmed in this pass; EU law, written before the EDPB's December 2024 opinion and before the UK's 2025 Act.
